entry.title: MyDetector.ai Deep Dive — Honest Experience with AI Detection and Humanizer
entry.summary:
Lately, I’ve been curious about how much of the content online is actually AI-generated. Some posts feel human, some feel… a bit robotic. I decided to try MyDetector.ai to see how it works in real life. After spending some time with it, here’s my experience, along with what I think could make it even better. The site opens cleanly and immediately feels easy to use. No signup, no clutter, just a space to paste text or upload an image. I tried a few blog paragraphs, social media posts, and even a meme generated by AI — the results appeared in seconds.
1. Fast and effortless 2. Everything in one place 3. Clean design
1. Explain results better 2. Keep a history of results 3. Show changes in humanizer clearly 4. Mobile and accessibility 5. Transparency about limits Compared to NoteGPT AI Detector and AIHumanizer, MyDetector.ai feels lighter and faster. It’s great for quick checks, while NoteGPT offers more features for handling full files, batch processing, and workflow integration. AIHumanizer focuses mostly on text, and its control options are limited compared to MyDetector’s humanizer. Use MyDetector.ai for quick checks on social posts, blog snippets, or emails. For longer documents or multiple files, consider combining it with NoteGPT to get more detailed feedback and batch capabilities. When using the humanizer, always read the revised text to ensure it keeps your original meaning and tone. Using MyDetector.ai felt like having a small helper for your writing. It’s fast, simple, and approachable — ideal for quickly checking whether content might be AI-generated or needs a more natural touch. With some improvements, like clearer explanations, history tracking, and a better humanizer view, it could become a tool you rely on every day. https://mydetector.ai

entry.title: My First Steps in JavaScript: A Simple Breakdown
entry.summary:
For the last two days, I’ve been learning the basics of JavaScript, and it has been really fun and easy to understand. These topics may look simple, but they are the building blocks for everything we will write in the future. So I wanted to share what I learned in a clear and beginner-friendly way. 1. Variables in JavaScript let Used for values that can change later.
let age = 20; age = 21;
const Used when the value should not be changed.
const PI = 3.14;
var The old way of declaring variables. Not recommended now because it creates confusion with scope. 2. Data Types in JavaScript Primitive Types String → "Hello"
Number → 23, 45.6
Boolean → true or false
Null → empty value Undefined → no value assigned BigInt → very large numbers Symbol → unique values Non-Primitive Types Object Array Function 3. Undefined vs Null undefined Means a variable exists but has no value yet.
let x; console.log(x); // undefined
null Means intentionally empty. We set it manually when something should have no value.
let data = null;

entry.title: The generative AI revolution promises productivity gains, but is it making us smarter or simply outsourcing our thinking?
entry.summary: The spectre haunting higher education today isn’t plagiarism. That’s a problem of ethics and detection, and we’ve largely figured that out. The new spectre is far more insidious, far more dangerous — it’s the spectre of perfect output and an empty mind. Picture this. You’re in a university seminar, and a student can, in seconds, conjure a 2,000-word essay on the geopolitical intricacies of the Treaty of Westphalia. The prose is impeccable, the arguments razor-sharp, the structure flawless. But then, the uncomfortable question arises — “Can you explain the third paragraph without looking at your screen?” The answer is often silence. We are living through a profound uncoupling of doing from understanding. For centuries, the very act of labour — writing, calculating, coding — was the crucible…

entry.title: Anthropic vs. OpenAI red teaming methods reveal different security priorities for enterprise AI
entry.summary: Model providers want to prove the security and robustness of their models, releasing system cards and conducting red-team exercises with each new release. But it can be difficult for enterprises to parse through the results, which vary widely and can be misleading.
